planting.note: Repot in spring just as new roots emerge from the base of the newest growth, using a coarse bark or lava-rock mix that drains within seconds of watering.

directions: Laelia purpurata is a large-flowered epiphyte from the coastal mountain forests of southern Brazil, celebrated as the country's national flower and used as a parent behind countless modern Cattleya-alliance hybrids. Club-shaped pseudobulbs each carry one or two broad, leathery leaves, and mature growths send up a spike of three to five flowers five to seven inches across, with white to soft rose-pink sepals and petals surrounding a dramatically flared, deep purple-magenta lip; growers prize dozens of named color forms ranging from pure white 'alba' to wine-dark 'werkhauseri'. Grow in strong, bright light with excellent air movement in a coarse bark or lava-rock mix, watering heavily while roots are active in the warm months and easing off after the late-spring to summer bloom. Botanists now classify this species in Cattleya as Cattleya purpurata, but the name Laelia purpurata remains the standard trade and collection name.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online
Marie Selby Botanical Gardens orchid collection notes

planting.note: Grow mounted on cork or in a shallow clay pot with coarse bark or rock chips, repotting in spring as new growth resumes after the plant's dry winter rest.

directions: Laelia gouldiana is a Mexican highland species now extinct in the wild, surviving today only in cultivation and often traced to plants long kept in village courtyards and church gardens near its former range in Hidalgo state. Cylindrical pseudobulbs topped by a single stiff leaf send up a tall winter spike carrying up to ten rounded, magenta-red flowers with a darker, white-throated lip veined in red, blooming reliably around the December holidays alongside its close relative Laelia anceps, with which it shares much of its culture and is sometimes hybridized. Grow mounted or in a very open, fast-draining mix in bright light, giving a pronounced dry rest with only occasional misting through late fall and winter until new roots appear in spring. Its tolerance of brief near-freezing nights makes it a good candidate for sheltered outdoor culture in the warmer Gulf Coast zones, much like Laelia anceps.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

common_name: Fiery Reed-Stem Orchid (Crucifix Orchid, Spice Orchid)

planting.note: Plant rooted keikis or divisions in spring into humus-rich, well-drained garden soil or a large container; established clumps tolerate brief light frost once mulched.

directions: Epidendrum ibaguense is a reed-stemmed, largely terrestrial species ranging from Mexico through northern South America, closely related to and often confused with Epidendrum radicans, with which it shares a nearly identical garden habit. Dense, rounded terminal clusters of small, spurless flowers in fiery orange, red, or yellow open atop upright canes almost year-round in warm climates, each bloom's lower lip splayed into a small cross shape that gives the plant its common name 'crucifix orchid'. It thrives in ordinary garden soil amended with bark and perlite for drainage, unlike most epiphytic orchids that demand specialized mounting or bark culture, and it roots readily from keikis that form along the cane. In zone 9b-11 Gulf Coast beds it makes a reliable, nearly maintenance-free perennial for full sun to light shade, attracting butterflies with its long bloom season.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
LSU AgCenter — Hardy Orchids for Gulf Coast Louisiana Landscapes

planting.note: Pot or mount in a fine, constantly damp bark-and-sphagnum mix; repot or divide only when the medium breaks down, since the fibrous roots resent disturbance.

directions: Masdevallia infracta is a tufted miniature epiphyte from cloud forests of Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia, distinguished from its showier cousins by nodding, triangular flowers in muted tones of maroon, ochre, and dull yellow-green, each sepal drawn into a short downward-curving tail that gives the flower a hooded, slightly nodding posture. It tolerates a somewhat wider temperature range than many Masdevallia species, making it a good entry point into the genus for growers with a cool, humid, air-conditioned room or shaded greenhouse rather than a full mountain-cool setup. Keep the fine bark-and-sphagnum medium evenly and constantly damp, since the plant has no pseudobulbs to buffer against drying, and maintain strong air movement to offset the high humidity it needs. Best grown as a shaded houseplant or greenhouse specimen rather than outdoors year-round.
sources: American Orchid Society — Masdevallia culture sheet
Ecuagenera Orquídeas del Ecuador — species reference

planting.note: Grow in a small pot or basket of chopped tree fern fiber, fir bark, and sphagnum; repot in spring only when the mix has broken down, as roots are easily damaged.

directions: Masdevallia caudata is a mini-miniature cloud-forest epiphyte from Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, and western Venezuela, named for the long, slender, whip-like tails that trail from the tips of its triangular sepals, giving each nearly six-inch flower a kite-like silhouette above the low tuft of leaves. Flower color runs from purplish-red to yellow-ochre with darker veining, and established clumps can carry several blooms at once through fall and winter. It needs cool-to-cold nights, deep shade, and high humidity with steady air movement to prevent rot, conditions best met in a shaded greenhouse or air-conditioned growing space rather than an average warm home. Pot in small containers or baskets favoring root aeration, and never allow the medium to dry out completely.
sources: American Orchid Society — Masdevallia culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Mount on rough bark or grow in a slatted basket with coarse, fast-draining mix; repot in spring as new roots emerge, giving a distinct dry rest through winter to encourage flowering.

directions: Encyclia cordigera grows naturally in dry coastal forests from Mexico south to Brazil, forming nearly spherical pseudobulbs topped by two thick, leathery leaves that taper into a long petiole-like base. A tall, upright spike carries several intensely fragrant, long-lasting flowers with narrow olive-brown to bronze sepals and petals surrounding a broad, heart-shaped lip in shades from deep magenta-purple to, in rarer color forms, near white. Its heavy, sweet fragrance and durable blooms make it one of the most collected Encyclia species, and it tolerates brighter light and higher heat than most orchids, reflecting its dry-forest origin. Water thoroughly during active spring and summer growth, then cut back sharply in winter to trigger the pronounced dry rest this species needs before its late-winter to spring bloom.
sources: Ecuagenera USA — Encyclia cordigera species profile
National Tropical Botanical Garden — clamshell orchid reference
